title: When AI Takes Notes: Court Allows Privacy Claims Against Otter.ai to Proceed

reading.body:
Otter.ai's transcription software records virtual meetings by default without obtaining consent from all participants, according to a federal lawsuit. The system is deployed in work contexts where participants may not realize recordings are occurring, and the plaintiffs allege the company uses these recordings to train its AI models without permission. A technical control that would have caught this is requiring affirmative consent from every meeting participant before recording begins, rather than relying on a checkbox in a privacy policy.

The case centers on whether default recording of group conversations violates wiretap and privacy laws, particularly when participants are unaware of the practice. The lawsuit alleges Otter uses the collected audio data to improve its transcription systems despite claiming to de-identify the recordings beforehand. What is not established is whether the de-identification process actually removes confidential information, whether the company's use of the data violates specific laws, or what legal obligations Otter has to obtain consent under applicable regulations.

summary:
A federal lawsuit filed in California accuses Otter.ai, a popular AI transcription service, of secretly recording private work conversations without permission. The company's software, which transcribes virtual meetings on platforms like Zoom and Google Meet, records discussions by default without asking all meeting participants for consent, according to the suit. Plaintiff Justin Brewer claims his privacy was severely violated when he discovered Otter was covertly recording a confidential conversation. The lawsuit alleges the company uses these recordings to train its artificial intelligence systems and gain financial benefit, violating state and federal privacy and wiretap laws.

The case highlights growing privacy concerns surrounding Otter, which now has 25 million users and has processed over one billion meetings since its founding in 2016. While Otter's privacy policy states users grant permission by checking a box, the lawsuit contends many people are still deceived. Recent incidents have included an AI researcher discovering Otter recorded sensitive investor discussions and a journalist learning the company shares user data with third parties. Otter claims it de-identifies audio before using it for machine learning, but the lawsuit questions whether this process effectively removes confidential information and guarantees anonymity.
